comments.name: Mr.Little

There is a religious revival;  the reasons for it given here are certainly important. The  great marble edifice of materialism is beginning to crack.  Here are a few other causes of this nascent paradigm shift:

First: The “Hard Problem of Consciousness “ is now considered one of the most important questions in science and philosophy.  The idea that consciousness is an “epiphenomenon of neural activity” is no longer an unquestioned assumption.  

Second: The 12-Step movement.  Alcoholics Anonymous introduced a “program of spiritual development” as a way out of addiction, and the non- dogmatic spiritual approach has caught fire over the nearly 100 years since the program started.

Third: The weird behavior of quantum particles- it is said to be unscientific to equate things like quantum entanglement and the changes in sub-atomic behavior according to whether or not the particles are being observed with spirituality, but no one has figured out how to square these phenomena with Newtonian physics.  

Fourth: Anomalies that threaten the current scientific paradigm.  Near-death experiences, out-of-body experiences, (both of which have furnished accounts featuring veridical evidence), psychic phenomena, including telepathic experiences, the behavior of UAP -Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena- objects of unknown origin that preform in ways that defy physics, all of this is getting harder to dismiss as nonsense.  

Maybe reality is not just matter.

Almost 80. Times have changed dramatically. We have three gen-x. All colleges were paid for by us. All got scholarship money. We borrowed HELO for the third. They all paid for their Masters + degree. They would anticipate the same futility and existential questions that all humans face, find no way forward, so not even try.

Perhaps the lesson we will learn is that one can be omniscient, yet still be hopelessly lost.

And maybe God isn't at all real, but AI technology and a future we can barely imagine is leading towards finally creating the very Supreme Being we've been looking for elsewhere. By then, though, there probably won't be any humans around to worship it. Not unlike what existed, or didn't, before the Big Bang.

New educational technology will deliver us from the mediocrity of the current system- and enable us to evolve our own improved intelligence faster than the "regression to the mean" AI/Machine Intelligence tech which has us all so fascinated today. We'll be able to predict storms, famines, pandemics, wars and revolutions in time to avoid their worst consequences. We'll be able to read the minds of our politicians by what they do and who pay for them instead of what they say they do. Why would anyone want to preserve an oppressively tedious job like coding, when a machine can do it for us in an instant and we can start to test its output immediately? I see all this fear mongering (crocodile tears) by the AI executives as a simple attempt at regulatory capture for the purpose of defending their own turf from competition. It won't happen because the Chinese won't let it happen. Welcome to the Brave New World. Like global warming, we have to adapt. Nobody's going to stop it no matter how we vote. Anyone who claims they can and will are lying to you.

comments.name: Rebecca
comments.body: I have three beautiful chests in my small NYC apartment - one for possessions from my childhood, one for items I kept of my mother's when she passed away and one for items that belonged to my sister's, who has also passed away. I also have other things I keep displayed - like books of theirs or drawings, and of course photos. I use things of theirs when I can. I have maybe one or two pieces of clothing. But that's it. It takes me hours and hours if I sit with things in these chests. I can't imagine having boxes of their stuff, certainly not stored in a storage unit. It would feel like a burden. Keeping the things I have in these chests and from their lives in the way I have makes them feel like treasures I can go through at any time. They are accessible. And I am reminded of other things all the time that I have given pride of place in my apartment (or when I use them - simple things like a mixing bowl). What is the point of keeping things locked away? And my life feels uncluttered and light and easy. I respect however people want to live their lives but I do think accumulating stuff is usually unhelpful even if it may feel like the easiest choice in the moment.

"Maybe we're born with it. Maybe it's Maybelline."

1942–1944: The parade was canceled because rubber and helium were needed for the war effort, particularly for military equipment and aircraft. 

1945: It returned, with roughly 2 million people coming out to see it. 

1971: There was a major weather disruption: the balloons were grounded, but the parade itself continued with floats and performers.

comments.name: Michael Fischer

As a University teacher I spent 40 years (all pre-GenAI) helping students improve their writing. The marking rubric was heavily focussed cumulatively on quality of facts (C level), quality of argument (B level), and ability to sustain an argument (A level). Although we would point out 'slop', such as 'it is important to argue that …', this did not impact the mark.

Everyone who needs to write needs to learn how to write. For some this comes easy, those who can naturally relate their thinking in words.  Not surprisingly, the latter are designating all such assisted content 'slop', rather than evaluating the content. The critical tells should not be em-dashes, but lousy ideas and lousy arguments. Good ideas will not emerge from GenAI without a lot of human supervision and direction. 

Suppression of AI assisted writing is lazy gatekeeping at best, a futile attempt to protect one's established turf, but because these people are gatekeepers they create suffering for others during this brief time they are in ascendence.

When PCs came in, we all had to adapt. Personally, I found the use of a word processor liberating. Complicated text edits could now be visualised and accomplished easily on screen. What on earth is wrong with being able to ‘easily undo,’ apparently some sort of writing sin?
Surely everyone likes a clean interface, which is why I dumped Microsoft products in favour of Apple’s elegant Pages. If your computer presents ‘blinking terminal windows,’ change brands - it doesn’t have to be that way!
This nostalgia for the typewriter reminds me that there are people who insist vinyl is better than CDs, that valve amplifiers sound ‘sweeter’ than transistor amplifiers, and that ICE cars have some mystical, (testosterone-based?) superiority to EVs. But all of that is a delusion too.

This is the most important part of the interview. 

“So then I start talking with the machine. I said, essentially, “Hey, here is something I published, here are all my unpublished files. Here is the research program of every single step for how this construction should go. Please build this thing.” Initially the machine didn’t believe me. Because the thing that we ended up proving, the thing that I thought was true for quite a while, was contrary to what everyone in the community thought.

Eventually the machine started believing me, and it built this thing. It’s ugly, and it’s all wrong. But just having the wrong thing is enough for us to build the correct thing, and that gave us the first paper. The final thing in the paper is purely human.”

The AI labs have been underselling the importance of the experts in the process of solving some of these complex problems, and in so doing promoting the narrative of Super Intelligent agents outperforming human ingenuity and creativity. 
The fact is that the machines are tools that amplify human intelligence, allowing us to develop solutions much faster than we could have otherwise. It is up to us to use the tools to our benefit because without us, they are not that smart.

Whatever the balance, or imbalance in the cooperative equation between the human and the ai “tool”, it is not going to stay the same. The ai of next year will be far in advance of the ones used by the professor this year. The AI’s that develop the following year will be even further advanced. Probably in ways impossible to predict. Possibly impossible to comprehend. The human participant will more or less be the same. Picture 2 children working on a problem. One grows incredibly fast, one doesn’t grow at all. Within a week the static child is working to solve the problem with a pre-teen. Within a month, with a fully developed adult. At which point does the contribution of the static child become useless? I don’t see the human factor in this partnership of solving math problems (or making art or designing buildings or fighting wars) as reliable. Before too long the human will be too far behind the ai to have anything to contribute. The ai “tools” will have evolved too far beyond to require the comparatively infantile input produced at mere human speed.

Book printing is certainly bifurcating - long-run printers use offset presses (that are increasingly difficult to staff), to print many thousands of books at minimal cost in a single run vs short-run digital printers (NOT necessarily POD) who can cost-effectively print one to a few thousand copies but can't compete on price for the very high-volume jobs. 

This article is really pointing to the growing challenge with offset printing businesses that supply huge volumes of books to the biggest publishers, especially on their best-selling titles. That's an important part of the book business, but it's been slowly shrinking because book publishing and consumer demand for books has fragmented massively over the last decades. 

Today, so many books are published that you are guaranteed to sell far fewer copies of a single title than ever before, on average. This moves demand for printing from long runs to short runs, making the offset print business more challenging. That trend feeds consolidation and facility closures, making the offset print supply chain more susceptible to these kinds of big delays when there are demand shocks. 

We see this play out everyday at Bookmobile.com in Minneapolis (short run digital book printing), where certain publishers look to us to provide precious inventory on books while they wait for their long runs to print. 

The question is whether this year's problem is symptomatic of the end of book printing as it was versus where it's going.

On September 1861, on the cusp of a winter storm in the North Atlantic, three men altered the fate of the world by pulling off one of the greatest acts of American espionage.

In England, cradle of the Industrial Revolution, the world's largest machine was created--a giant iron steamship 60 years ahead of its time. The Scientific American warned that this colossus "could run down the whole of the largest steamers in any other fleet, one after another, without firing a single shot."

The mission of the three Americans was to stop this colossus from entering a southern port without anyone ever knowing what transpired. And end the Civil War with a Confederate victory.

Inspired by true events, The Leviathan is a story of treason, espionage, and geopolitics; a family sundered by the conflict between the states; and of British capitalists lusting to dismember the United States for their own benefit.

But in most of the animal kingdom males are blissfully uninterested in sex except when they encounter a female in heat when they become hyperfocused.  Humans are exceptions though because we are aware of what we are doing when we have sex and also because we have sex for enjoyment.  The high levels of testosterone in males explains why we are always indiscriminately ogling women.  Women tend to not engage in this sort of behavior as constantly as men do.  But it is interesting to see this becoming a cultural phenomenon in China.  Perhaps they will understand the constant low level of sexual frustration that men experience every day.
